root.note: Built on fābula ‘story, talk’, from the old Latin verb for ‘to say’.

history: When you hablar, you are technically telling tales. Latin fābula was a story, and fābulārī meant to tell stories, then simply to chat. In medieval Castilian the word was fablar. Later the f- turned into an h, which is now silent: the same thing happened in hacer and hervir. Spanish and Portuguese (falar) are the only Romance languages to use this root for ‘to speak’. French parler and Italian parlare come from a different word, Greek parabola, which Christian Latin used for a comparison and later for talk. Fábula and fabuloso are the same family, taken later straight from Latin, with the f intact.
historyEinfach: Hablar means ‘to speak’. In Latin, fabula meant ‘a story’. The Latin verb meant ‘to tell stories’, and then ‘to talk’. In old Spanish the word was fablar. Later the f became h, and now we do not say the h. Portuguese falar is the same word. French parler is a different word.

elsewhere.text: Portuguese keeps the f that Spanish lost. Set side by side, falar and hablar show you the old Spanish change.
French took another road: a Greek word for comparison came to mean simply speaking.
Italian parlare is the same word as French parler, and unrelated to hablar.
